comments.author: @AustinGlamourPhoto
comments.text: It's still completely in the realm of the abstract. Human intelligence evolved to manipulate objects in the environment. LLM think in terms of language tokens. The human mind thinks in terms of objects. Specifically the human mind predicts the motion of objects and estimates the necessary force and vector to apply in order to control and place objects in space and time. That's what human intelligence is. If you think about chess, you are predicting the motion and placement of the enemies pieces and you are estimating correctly where to place your own pieces in order to win the game. This is so simple it's hard for abstract academic to wrap their head around it. Playing basketball is another example. A player has to make many many quick decisions to control the motion of his own body and the motion of the ball while predicting the motion of the enemy players and while estimating the correct amount of force and vector to apply to the ball in order to place it in the basket or take the ball away form the enemy. This gets into game theory as both teams are attempting to control and place the ball. Same thing with driving a car. It's actually the same thing with running a major corporation. Human intelligence evolved to control analog reality and digital is not real. P.S. - I just gave you gave you the formula to AGI and it's not language tokens.

comments.author: @tinyhato
comments.text:
Regarding AI progress, I notice that Wes often points out that people in the field (who should know) are just following the data points, so therefore AI progress will just keep going.  I just want to try to address some of the possible reasons why this isn't doing anything to quell the doubters.  First, the motives of the people in the field.  If they say that progress is slowing, the money stops coming in.  So to people who believe that these researchers want to keep their jobs more than they want to be honest with the public, the argument that these smart people who know more about it than anyone are saying something is *literally meaningless*.  One could argue the merits of never trusting anyone who comments on the place where they work, but that is the state of things from a lot of people.

Second, the exponential.  When I first heard "following the exponential" it was about scaling compute, because none of the breakthroughs that came about in the past couple of years had happened. So I think the belief is that if scaling isn't going to do it alone, then there is no guarantee that the exponential will continue, because scaling is the only thing that we can guarantee. There is no guarantee of breakthroughs. Even if one thinks it likely that there are many more breakthroughs to be had, pointing at an exponential curve and saying "this is going to happen" when it requires both known- and unknown-unknowns to be discovered and overcome can seem hopeful to some and not something to be taken with certainty. In other words, the willingness to follow this curve requires accepting a very large "IF", which I don't think I have ever heard mentioned when someone points to it.

comments.author: @5zzz
comments.text:
Wes, this video about the victims of AI is, ironically, the perfect example of the trend itself. The primary victim, for my workflow, is a specific type of long-form video format: the secondary-source summary.

Here’s my new reality: I'm subscribed, but I no longer watch videos like this one. I take the link, give it to an AI (like Gemini), and get a perfect summary of the core claims in seconds. This has led me to a new rule for media in the AI age, where I see two distinct types of content:

1.  *Secondary/Summary Content:* Videos that analyze or review existing information (like this one). AI now does this faster and more efficiently, allowing me to launch my own research.
2.  *Primary/Experiential Content:* Videos that document a unique, real-world event, a journey, or an authentic human interaction. This is irreplaceable raw data, and the only format worth watching in full.

Your content, as insightful as it is, falls squarely into the first category. It’s an expert summary of other people's work and ideas.

So when you discuss who gets impacted, my viewing habit is the evidence. Your role as a presenter of secondary information is being replaced by AI-powered tools that let me do my own active research. You provide the initial prompt, but the deep dive is now a solo, high-speed process.

A fascinating, real-time example of the very disruption you're covering.
